did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jerusalem is portrayed here as a human figure: a city that was once great among the nations and a princess among the provinces, but has become lonely like a widow and enslaved.
Did you know? This verse describes Judah’s exile and her restless wandering among the nations; even her pursuers overtake her in narrow places.
Did you know? The desolation of Jerusalem is evident throughout the city: the roads to Zion mourn, the gates lie deserted, the priests sigh, and the young women grieve.
Did you know? The lament connects the destruction with Jerusalem’s sins, describing her enemies as having risen to power over her and her children as having been taken captive.
Did you know? The nations’ entry into the sanctuary is portrayed as a serious desecration because they entered a place the Torah forbade them to enter as part of the congregation.
Did you know? The famine in Jerusalem was so severe that its inhabitants gave their precious possessions in exchange for food to restore their lives.
Did you know? Jerusalem appeals to passersby and asks them to look upon her suffering, which she says is unlike any other pain.
Did you know? The lament emphasizes Jerusalem’s loneliness: her comforter has moved far from her, and her children have become desolate because the enemy has prevailed.
Did you know? Jerusalem acknowledges the LORD’s righteousness and confesses that she rebelled against His word; in the same verse, she describes the exile of her young women and young men.
Did you know? The description of the disaster encompasses every area of life: outside, the sword brings death, and inside, death reigns; therefore Jerusalem asks the LORD to see her distress.
